title: Chapter 4 — Controlling Access to Files with ACLs
display: Chapter 4 — Controlling Access to Files with ACLs

content.text: By the end of this chapter, you should understand how Linux controls access to files and directories using Access Control Lists (ACLs).
Understand the ACL mask and permission precedence.
Add, change and remove ACL entries.
Configure default ACLs so new files and directories inherit permissions.
Verify permissions and practise realistic administration tasks.
The main idea is simple: ACLs allow you to give different permissions to additional users and groups without changing the owner of a file.
ACL stands for Access Control List.
Linux normally uses three main permission categories:
Owner: The user who owns the file.
Group: The group associated with the file.
Others: Everyone else who is not covered by the applicable owner or group permissions.
For example, suppose a file belongs to the user alice and the group developers.
Alice to read and edit the file.
Members of developers to read the file.
A second user, bob, to read the file.
Everyone else to have no access.
Ordinary owner, group and other permissions may not express all these requirements conveniently. ACLs let you add a separate permission entry for Bob without changing the file's owner or group.
Think of ordinary permissions as three access lists. ACLs let you add more specific entries for named users and groups.
2. Understand read, write and execute permissions
ACLs use the same basic permissions as ordinary Linux file permissions.
Create, remove or rename entries, subject to other restrictions
A user may have permission to read a directory's listing but still be unable to enter it if the user lacks execute permission.
Also, a user generally needs execute permission on the directory path leading to a file to access that file.
Named user: An additional user who receives a specific ACL entry.
Named group: An additional group that receives a specific ACL entry.
Default ACL: An ACL attached to a directory that provides permission settings inherited by newly created files and subdirectories.
ACL mask: A limit on the effective permissions of named users, the owning group and named groups. It does not limit the file owner's permissions or the permissions assigned to others.
Remember that the mask can reduce the effective permissions granted by an ACL entry.
4. Check whether a file has an ACL
A file with an extended ACL commonly shows a plus sign (+) after its permission string.
The + indicates that additional access-control information exists.
However, ls -l does not explain every ACL entry. Use getfacl for the full details.
This displays the file's ACL entries, including the owner, owning group, named users or groups, mask and other permissions when applicable.
To inspect a file and its directory:
The -d option with ls displays information about the directory itself rather than listing its contents.
user::rw- — the file owner has read and write permissions.
user:bob:r-- — Bob has a named-user ACL entry granting read permission.
group::r-- — the owning group has read permission.
mask::r-- — the maximum effective permissions for mask-controlled entries are read-only.
other::--- — other users have no permissions.
The empty name in user:: identifies the file owner. Similarly, group:: identifies the owning group.
Important: An ACL entry is not always the same as the effective permission. You must also check the mask when one applies.
The mask sets the maximum effective permissions for:
Named users, excluding the file owner.
Bob's entry requests read, write and execute permissions, but the mask permits only read access.
Therefore, Bob's effective permission is r--.
The mask does not restrict the file owner's permissions or the other entry.
The mask can be calculated automatically when ACL entries are modified. You can also set it explicitly.

When Linux checks whether a user can access a file, it evaluates the applicable permission category.
If the user owns the file, the owner's ACL entry applies.
Otherwise, if the user has a matching named-user entry, that entry applies, subject to the mask.
Otherwise, if the user's groups match the owning group or a named-group entry, the applicable group permissions apply, subject to the mask.
If none of these categories applies, the other permissions apply.
Do not assume Linux simply adds every permission together. The applicable category and the ACL mask determine the result.
ACLs are useful when a system needs more flexible access control than the traditional owner/group/other model.
For example, systemd's journal files can use ACLs to grant selected groups read access to logs without making those files generally readable by everyone.
RHEL filesystems must support ACLs, and the filesystem must be mounted with ACL support enabled. XFS supports ACLs and is commonly used by RHEL.
9. Add or modify an ACL entry
The setfacl command manages ACL permissions.

You should see an entry for Bob.
Suppose the group developers needs read and write access to a file.

Remember: Adding a named-group entry does not change the file's owner or owning group.
Suppose you want to apply an ACL to a directory and its existing contents.
-m modifies or adds an ACL entry.
u:bob:r-X gives Bob read permission and conditional execute permission.
The uppercase X is important. It adds execute permission to directories and preserves or grants execute permission to regular files according to the conditional rules of X.
This helps users search directories without unnecessarily making every regular file executable.

For a directory, -b also removes its extended access ACL entries, but it does not remove its default ACL. Use -k to remove the default ACL.

A normal ACL controls access to the file or directory on which it is set.
A default ACL on a directory provides permission settings that newly created files and subdirectories can inherit.
Imagine that a shared project directory is used by several team members. You want new content created inside that directory to receive suitable access permissions automatically.
Without a default ACL, you might need to adjust every new file separately.
A default ACL helps establish the intended permission rules for new content.
Important: A default ACL controls inheritance. It does not itself grant access to the directory on which it is configured. The directory still needs appropriate access ACL entries.

Default permissions are inherited by newly created content, but the final permissions also depend on the type of object created and the permissions requested when it is created.

For example, regular files do not automatically become executable merely because a default ACL includes execute permission. Newly created regular files normally do not receive execute permission when their creation mode excludes it.

18. Understand ACL inheritance and directory access
Suppose /shared has a default ACL for the developers group.
When a user creates a new file or subdirectory inside /shared, the new object can inherit ACL entries from the parent directory's default ACL.
However, inheritance does not mean every new object receives identical effective permissions in every situation. The requested creation permissions and the type of object matter.
Also remember that users need permission to search the parent directories in the path. An ACL on a file does not bypass restrictions on the directories leading to it.

Checking only ls -l: Use getfacl to inspect extended ACL entries.
Ignoring the mask: A named user or group can have fewer effective permissions than its ACL entry appears to grant.
Confusing default ACLs with access ACLs: Default ACLs control inheritance; they do not replace the permissions required to access the directory itself.
Forgetting directory execute permission: Users generally need execute permission on directories in the path to reach a file.
Using recursive changes without checking the target: Recursive changes can alter many files and directories.
Assuming new files become executable: File creation modes can limit inherited permissions.
Removing the wrong entries: Understand the difference between -x, -b and -k before changing a live system.

ACLs extend the traditional Linux owner, group and other permission model.
getfacl displays ACL entries and effective permissions.
setfacl -m adds or modifies ACL entries.
The ACL mask limits effective permissions for named users, the owning group and named groups.
Default ACLs provide permission settings for new files and subdirectories.
setfacl -x removes selected entries, setfacl -b removes extended access ACL entries, and setfacl -k removes default ACL entries.
Always verify your changes with getfacl and test the intended access in a safe lab.
The central lesson of Chapter 4 is that ACLs let administrators manage detailed file and directory access without having to rely only on the traditional owner, group and other permissions.
